Pure linear projection connectors ($\pi_0$) apply a single linear layer that maps each patch independently. No cross-token interaction occurs during projection, so tokens are genuinely independent. Removing one token loses approximately $1/N$ of the visual field, and the loss is spatially uniform.

X-VLA complicates this picture. Its connector is nominally a linear projection, but vision tokens subsequently pass through a 12-layer BART encoder~\cite{lewis2020bart} before reaching the LLM. The BART encoder's self-attention layers introduce cross-token mixing that creates partial dependencies: X-VLA's CV (0.151) is four times higher than $\pi_0$'s (0.038), and its attention entropy (0.614) is substantially lower. This explains X-VLA's threshold-graded pattern: the BART encoder differentiates tokens enough that removing 30\% crosses a threshold, but not enough to cause degradation at 10\% removal. The nominal connector label (``linear projection'') is insufficient; the effective pipeline complexity---including any post-connector processing---determines pruning tolerance.

MLP projectors (OpenVLA, OFT) process each patch through a 3-layer MLP with GELU activations. Per-patch processing preserves spatial locality, but non-linear transformations create partial dependencies between each projected representation and the broader feature space. The result is an intermediate regime: tokens carry differentiated information without the rigid spatial entanglement of pixel-shuffle.

The coefficient of variation (CV) of token importance, measured as the variation in L2 norms across vision tokens, captures the heterogeneity that determines pruning tolerance. CV forms a continuous spectrum across the four measured models: $\pi_0$ CV $= 0.038$ (tokens carry near-equal importance), X-VLA CV $= 0.151$ (mild differentiation), OpenVLA CV $= 0.215$ (moderate differentiation), SmolVLA CV $= 0.314$ (high heterogeneity). This ordering predicts not just the class of degradation but the onset point: $\pi_0$ (CV $= 0.038$) is immune through $k{=}0.1$, X-VLA (CV $= 0.151$) is robust until $k{=}0.7$ then cliffs, OpenVLA (CV $= 0.215$) degrades from $k{=}0.95$, and SmolVLA (CV $= 0.314$) collapses at $k{=}0.95$.

Attention entropy provides the mechanistic explanation for why CV predicts pruning behavior. $\pi_0$ attention entropy is 0.9999, near-maximally uniform across all 18 layers (range 0.931--0.983). When all tokens contribute equally, any subset preserves a proportional share of the total information, and the model can redistribute attention without loss. Low CV combined with high entropy means tokens are interchangeable: removing any subset is equivalent to uniform downsampling.

SmolVLA presents an apparent paradox. Its attention entropy is also high (0.952, range 0.93--0.98, spread 0.05), yet pruning is catastrophic. The resolution lies in the combination of high entropy with high CV: tokens are uniformly attended (the model treats them all as necessary) but carry heterogeneous spatial content due to pixel-shuffle folding. The model cannot selectively attend to a subset because all tokens are equally demanded, yet the tokens themselves are not interchangeable. This ``differentiated but entangled'' pattern is the signature of pixel-shuffle connectors: uniform attention over non-uniform content.

X-VLA occupies a revealing intermediate position. Its CV ($0.151$) falls between $\pi_0$ and OpenVLA, and its attention entropy ($0.614$) is the lowest among the four models. The 12-layer BART encoder introduces cross-token mixing that partially differentiates tokens, creating enough heterogeneity to trigger a cliff at $k{=}0.7$ but not enough to cause degradation at $k{=}0.9$. X-VLA demonstrates that CV predicts the \emph{onset point} of degradation, not merely a categorical class.

The aggregate $3.4\times$ action error increase (Table~\ref{tab:offline_action_error}, Appendix~\ref{app:offline_error}) is a clear negative signal, but per-step metrics do not distinguish moderate perturbations (position errors of 0.20--0.30 per axis) from catastrophic events (complete gripper inversion, L2 $= 1.02$) that individually terminate an episode. In closed-loop execution, a single catastrophic action pushes the robot off-trajectory, subsequent observations diverge from training data, and recovery becomes impossible. These events are rare enough to be diluted in per-step averages but occur in every pruned episode we tested.

X-VLA provides a concrete example of this disconnect. At $k{=}0.3$, X-VLA's offline normalized action loss is 1.0014, near the unpruned baseline, suggesting negligible degradation. Yet closed-loop SR at $k{=}0.3$ is 23.0\%, a 77pp drop from baseline, and even at the less aggressive $k{=}0.7$ the cliff to 56.2\% is already severe. Offline metrics register the average perturbation but not the task-level failures that dominate closed-loop outcomes. \paragraph{VLA token compression.}
Recent concurrent works achieve efficient token compression on MLP-projector VLAs. Compressor-VLA~\cite{gao2025compressorvla} uses instruction-guided cross-attention compression on OpenVLA-OFT~\cite{kim2025openoft}. SpecPrune-VLA~\cite{wang2025specprunevla} applies action-aware self-speculative pruning to OpenVLA with real-robot validation. LightVLA~\cite{jiang2026lightvla} introduces differentiable token pruning for VLA efficiency. ``See What Matters''~\cite{feng2026seewhatmatters} proposes grid-based continuous resampling on $\pi_0$ and SmolVLA, focusing on the discrete-versus-continuous sampling paradigm rather than connector-dependent failure modes. SparseVLM~\cite{zhang2025sparsevlm} and SparseVILA~\cite{khaki2025sparsevila} explore token sparsification in VLMs, and ``Don't Run with Scissors''~\cite{jabbour2025dontrun} examines weight pruning fragility in VLAs. All compression methods above operate on MLP-projector architectures or evaluate pruning without diagnosing connector-dependent failure modes. Our work is complementary: we identify why deletion-based approaches catastrophically fail on pixel-shuffle architectures, a failure mode not examined by prior work, and validate re-encoding as a remedy.

\paragraph{VLA token compression.}
Concurrent works compress tokens on MLP-projector VLAs: Compressor-VLA~\cite{gao2025compressorvla}, SpecPrune-VLA~\cite{wang2025specprunevla}, LightVLA~\cite{jiang2026lightvla}, and ``See What Matters''~\cite{feng2026seewhatmatters}. SparseVLM~\cite{zhang2025sparsevlm}, SparseVILA~\cite{khaki2025sparsevila}, and ``Don't Run with Scissors''~\cite{jabbour2025dontrun} explore sparsification and weight pruning fragility. All operate on MLP-projector architectures or evaluate without diagnosing connector-dependent failure modes. We identify why deletion catastrophically fails on pixel-shuffle architectures and validate re-encoding as a remedy.

\paragraph{$\pi_0$.} Measured on 100 frames from LIBERO-Object (tasks 20--29) across all 18 layers of the Gemma-based PaliGemma backbone (512 vision tokens: 256 per image $\times$ 2 cameras). The mean suffix-to-vision entropy ratio is 0.959 (range: 0.931--0.983, std 0.013), near-uniform across all layers with no progressive sharpening:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item All 18 layers: 0.931--0.983 (spread 0.052)
    \item Minimum: 0.931; Maximum: 0.983
\end{itemize}
The flat entropy profile, combined with $\pi_0$'s extremely low CV (0.038), explains its immunity to pruning: tokens carry near-equal importance and receive near-equal attention. Removing any subset is equivalent to uniform spatial downsampling, preserving a proportional share of the visual field without disrupting the attention distribution.
